questions.q: Explain the origin and meaning of the names 'Bharat' and 'Bharatavarsha'.
answer: Bharat is one of the oldest names for the subcontinent, and Bharatavarsha means "the land (varsha) of Bharata."

answer.text: Indian traditions connect the name to figures called Bharata — the son of Rishabha in the Jain tradition, and, in the epic tradition, the son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala.
The Bharatas were also an important jana (people) mentioned in the Rigveda, whose name came to be applied to the wider land.
In ancient geography, varsha meant a region or land, so Bharatavarsha expressed the idea of one land stretching across the subcontinent — an early sense of a shared identity.

questions.q: How did the names 'Hind', 'Hindustan' and 'India' originate?
answer: All three names trace back to a single river — the Sindhu (Indus).

answer.text: The Persians, on the north-western frontier, pronounced Sindhu as "Hindu," and the land beyond the river became Hind, and later Hindustan.
The Greeks wrote the river's name as Indos, from which came the name India for the land.
The Arabs called the region Al-Hind.

answer: Thus "Hindu," "Hind" and "India" were originally geographical names derived from the river Sindhu, not names of a religion.

questions.q: What is meant by Jambudvipa and Sapta-Sindhu?

answer.text: It means "the land or island (dvipa) of the jambu (rose-apple) tree." It was an ancient name for the subcontinent, used in the Puranas and in the inscriptions of Ashoka, reflecting a view of the land from within its own traditions.
It means "the land of seven rivers," a name used in the Rigveda for the north-western region watered by the Sindhu and its tributaries.

answer: Both names show that people in ancient times already had a sense of their land as a distinct geographical and cultural whole, named after its trees and its rivers.

questions.q: "India, that is Bharat." Discuss how the many names of the country reflect a shared civilisational identity.
answer: The country has carried many names — Bharat, Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Aryavarta, Hind, Hindustan and India — yet all point to the same land.

answer.text: Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa and Aryavarta arose within Indian traditions and expressed the idea of one land with a shared culture, sacred geography and pilgrimage network.
Hind, India and the Mesopotamian Meluhha were names given by outsiders — Persians, Greeks and others — after the river Sindhu or through trade contact.

That so many peoples, in so many languages, named this single land shows a long-recognised civilisational unity. The Constitution captures it in Article 1: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

questions.q: What was Aryavarta, and what do the various regional names of the land tell us?

answer.text: Aryavarta, meaning the land of the Aryas or noble people, was an ancient name for the northern part of the subcontinent, especially the region of the Ganga plains. It was one of several names by which different parts of the land were known in early texts.

Besides Aryavarta, the land was called Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa, while its rivers gave it the name Sapta-Sindhu, the land of seven rivers. Foreigners called it Hind, Hindustan and India after the river Sindhu.

These many names show that the idea of the land grew gradually and was seen from many angles, by its own people and by outsiders. Yet the names also reveal a shared sense of one great land, bound together by its rivers, mountains and traditions.

answer: Thus the variety of names reflects both India's diversity and its underlying unity.

questions.q: How did the name of the river Sindhu travel to distant lands and become 'India'?

answer.text: The name India goes back to the great river Sindhu, today called the Indus, which flows in the north-west of the subcontinent. To the people who lived beyond it, this river marked the beginning of the land.

The ancient Persians, who found it hard to pronounce the sound 's', changed Sindhu into Hindu, and used it for the river and the land beyond it. From this came the names Hind and Hindustan, still used today.
The Greeks, learning the name from the Persians, dropped the 'h' and called the river Indos and the land India. Through the Greeks and later the Europeans, the name India spread across the world.

answer: Thus a single river's name travelled from Persia to Greece and on to the whole world, becoming the country's best-known name.
